title: Mensuration (3D)
summary: Volumes and surface areas of cubes, cuboids, cylinders, cones, spheres, hemispheres, prisms and pyramids, plus melting-recasting, capacities and painted-cube counts. About 1-3 questions per shift; every question reduces to one formula plus a unit conversion, so memorising the formula sheet is nearly the whole job.

subtopics.title: Cube and cuboid
subtopics.concept:
For a cube of edge $a$ and a cuboid $l\times b\times h$:

| Quantity | Cuboid | Cube |
|---|---|---|
| Volume | $lbh$ | $a^3$ |
| Lateral (4 walls) | $2(l+b)h$ | $4a^2$ |
| Total surface | $2(lb+bh+lh)$ | $6a^2$ |
| Space diagonal | $\sqrt{l^2+b^2+h^2}$ | $a\sqrt3$ |

The space diagonal is the **longest rod that fits in the room**. Wall questions use the lateral area only.

tricks.title: Longest rod = space diagonal
tricks.body:
A rod can poke corner-to-corner through the room: $\sqrt{l^2+b^2+h^2}$. Triplets like (3,4,12,13) exist:
$3^2+4^2+12^2=169=13^2$.

example.q: Find the length of the longest rod that can be placed in a room of dimensions $12\text{ m}\times9\text{ m}\times8\text{ m}$.

tricks.title: Painting/flooring picks the right area
tricks.body: Four walls → $2(l+b)h$ (ignore floor and roof). Full painting including roof and floor → TSA. Cost = area × rate.

example.q: A room is 8 m long, 6 m wide and 4 m high. Find the cost of painting its four walls at ₹10 per sq m.

mistakes: Using TSA where the question asks only for the four walls (or the reverse).
Cube diagonal $a\sqrt3$ confused with the face diagonal $a\sqrt2$.
Height left out of the wall formula: walls need $h$; floor area does not.

subtopics.title: Cylinder
subtopics.concept:
For a cylinder of radius $r$ and height $h$:
- Volume $=\pi r^2h$ (capacity in litres: multiply $\text{m}^3$ by 1000)
- Curved surface $=2\pi rh$
- Total surface $=2\pi r(r+h)$
- A **hollow pipe/well** of inner radius $r$, outer radius $R$: volume of material $=\pi(R^2-r^2)h$
- A **wire/rod** is a very long thin cylinder: its volume is $\pi r^2\times\text{length}$.

tricks.title: 1 m³ = 1000 litres
tricks.body: Tank answers in litres: compute $\pi r^2h$ in metres, then ×1000. Keep radii in the units the answer needs.

example.q: A cylindrical water tank has a radius of 2 m and a depth of 7 m. Find its capacity in litres. [Use $\pi=\frac{22}{7}$]

tricks.title: Hollow cylinder: difference of squared radii
tricks.body: Material volume $=\pi(R^2-r^2)h$ — the cross-section is a ring.

example.q: A metallic pipe has inner radius 3 cm, outer radius 5 cm and length 14 cm. Find the volume of metal. [Use $\pi=\frac{22}{7}$]

mistakes: Using the outer radius alone for a hollow pipe.
Forgetting the 1000 factor when the answer is asked in litres.
CSA ($2\pi rh$) and TSA ($2\pi r(r+h)$) mixed up when the question mentions a closed drum or an open tank.

subtopics.title: Cone
subtopics.concept:
For a cone of radius $r$, height $h$ and slant height $\ell=\sqrt{r^2+h^2}$:
- Volume $=\frac13\pi r^2h$ (exactly one-third of the cylinder on the same base)
- Curved surface $=\pi r\ell$
- Total surface $=\pi r(\ell+r)$
- If a cone is rolled from a sector of a circle: the sector's radius is $\ell$, and arc length $=2\pi r$.

The $r$-$h$-$\ell$ triangle is right-angled, so Pythagorean triplets (3,4,5), (7,24,25), (5,12,13) appear constantly.

tricks.title: Triplet for the slant height
tricks.body: Check for (3,4,5) or (7,24,25) among $r,h,\ell$ before computing a square root.

example.q: The radius of a cone is 7 cm and its height 24 cm. Find its curved surface area. [Use $\pi=\frac{22}{7}$]

tricks.title: One-third of the cylinder
tricks.body:
Equal base and height: $V_{\text{cone}}=\frac13V_{\text{cylinder}}$ — useful directly in ratio questions and for
conical heaps of sand/grain.

example.q: A conical tent has base radius 7 m and height 24 m. Find its volume. [Use $\pi=\frac{22}{7}$]

mistakes: Using $\pi r^2h$ (cylinder volume) for a cone — the one-third is forgotten most often.
Rounding $\ell$ from a non-triplet when exact fractions were expected.

subtopics.title: Sphere and hemisphere
subtopics.concept:
- Sphere (radius $r$): volume $=\frac43\pi r^3$, surface $=4\pi r^2$.
- Hemisphere: volume $=\frac23\pi r^3$; curved surface $=2\pi r^2$; **total** surface $=3\pi r^2$ (adds the flat circular face).
- Melting and recasting conserves **volume** (surface area almost never matches — that option is a trap).

formulas.name: Hemisphere
formulas.tex: V=\frac23\pi r^3,\quad S_{\text{curved}}=2\pi r^2,\quad S_{\text{total}}=3\pi r^2

tricks.title: Count small balls by the cube of the radius ratio
tricks.body: Number of small spheres $=\left(\frac{R}{r}\right)^3$. Radii in ratio 8:1 → 512 pieces, no π needed.

example.q: A solid metallic sphere of radius 8 cm is melted and drawn into small spheres of radius 1 cm. How many are formed?

tricks.title: Hemisphere TSA is three circles
tricks.body: $3\pi r^2$: two for the curved half (recall the sphere is $4\pi r^2$) plus one for the base.

example.q: Find the total surface area of a solid hemisphere of radius 7 cm. [Use $\pi=\frac{22}{7}$]

mistakes: Hemisphere TSA taken as $2\pi r^2$ (that is the curved part only).
Melting questions answered with equality of surface areas.
$\frac43\pi r^3$ misremembered as $\frac{4\pi r^3}{3\text{ or }2}$ variants — write the fraction before substituting.

subtopics.title: Prisms, pyramids and painted cubes
subtopics.concept:
- **Prism:** two parallel congruent bases; volume $=$ base area $\times$ height.
- **Pyramid:** volume $=\frac13\times$ base area $\times$ height.
- **Painted cube cut into $n^3$ unit cubes** (side $n$): cubes with 3 painted faces $=8$ (corners);
  2 faces $=12(n-2)$ (edges); 1 face $=6(n-2)^2$; unpainted $=(n-2)^3$.

tricks.title: Painted-cube formula table
tricks.body: Identify $n$ = number of small cubes along one edge. Corners are fixed at 8; the rest depend on $n-2$.

example.q: A cube of side 7 cm is painted on all faces and cut into 1 cm cubes. How many small cubes have exactly two faces painted?

tricks.title: Pyramid by one-third
tricks.body: Same base and height as a prism: the pyramid holds exactly one-third.

example.q: A pyramid stands on a square base of side 10 cm and is 12 cm high. Find its volume.

mistakes: Forgetting the $\frac13$ in pyramid (and cone) volumes.
Painted-cube formulas applied with $n$ = side length in cm instead of cubes per edge.
Counting corner cubes as 6 or edge cubes as $12(n-1)$.

pyqPatterns.pattern: Four walls / cost of painting a room
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Room dimensions and a rate per sq m for painting walls or plastering.
pyqPatterns.approach: LSA $=2(l+b)h$; multiply by rate. Roof/floor included only if stated.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A sphere/cone/cylinder melted and recast into another shape; find a dimension or the count of pieces.
pyqPatterns.approach: Equate volumes; for counts use the cube of the radius (or side) ratio. Ignore surface area completely.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Cylindrical or cuboidal tank; capacity asked in litres.
pyqPatterns.approach: $\pi r^2h$ (or $lbh$) in m³, then ×1000; watch cm-to-m conversions.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Radius and height given as (3,4), (6,8), (7,24); asked for CSA/TSA or volume.
pyqPatterns.approach: $\ell$ from the triplet, then $\pi r\ell$; volume keeps $\frac13$.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Longest pole/rod inside a room or cube.

pyqPatterns.pattern: Painted cube cut into small cubes
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A painted cube is cut into equal small cubes; count cubes with 0/1/2/3 painted faces.
Sides of a cube change by x%; find the change in volume (or surface).
pyqPatterns.approach: Volume factor $(1+x/100)^3$, surface factor $(1+x/100)^2$. +10% → +33.1% volume, +21% surface.

solvedExamples.q: A room is 12 m long, 9 m wide and 8 m high. Find the length of the longest pole that can be placed inside the room.
solvedExamples.solution:
The longest pole fits along the space diagonal:

$\sqrt{12^2+9^2+8^2}=\sqrt{144+81+64}=\sqrt{289}=17$ m.
solvedExamples.shortcut: 12-9-8 → 17 is a stock diagonal: $144+81+64=289=17^2$. Trap: 15 m is the floor diagonal $\sqrt{12^2+9^2}$.

solvedExamples.q: A cylindrical tank of radius 2 m and depth 7 m is full of water. The capacity of the tank is: [Use $\pi=\frac{22}{7}$]
solvedExamples.solution:
$V=\pi r^2h=\frac{22}{7}\times4\times7=88$ m$^3$.

$1$ m$^3=1000$ litres, so capacity $=88{,}000$ litres.
solvedExamples.shortcut: $88$ m³ ×1000 → 88,000 L. Trap: 880 (×10) or answering in m³.

solvedExamples.q: A solid metallic cone of radius 6 cm and height 3 cm is melted and recast into a sphere. The radius of the sphere is:
solvedExamples.shortcut: $V_{\text{cone}}=36\pi$; set $\frac43\pi R^3=36\pi$ → $R^3=27$ → 3 cm. Trap: 6 cm (radius unchanged) and 2 cm (took $R^3=36/4$ with a slip).

solvedExamples.q: If each edge of a cube increases by 10%, the percentage increase in its volume is:
solvedExamples.solution:
Volume scales as the cube of the linear factor: $(1.1)^3=1.331$.

Increase $=33.1\%$. (Surface would rise by $(1.1)^2=1.21$, i.e. 21%.)

practice.q: The volume of a cube of edge 6 cm is:
The total surface area of a cuboid of dimensions $8\text{ cm}\times6\text{ cm}\times4\text{ cm}$ is:
practice.shortcut: Half of 208 is 104 — the bracket sum; double it. Trap: 104 (no doubling).

practice.q: The volume of a cylinder of radius 7 cm and height 10 cm is: [Use $\pi=\frac{22}{7}$]
The surface area of a sphere of radius 7 cm is: [Use $\pi=\frac{22}{7}$]
practice.shortcut: $4\times154=616$. Trap: 462 is the hemisphere TSA ($3\pi r^2$); 308 is $2\pi r^2$.

practice.q: The total surface area of a solid hemisphere of radius 7 cm is: [Use $\pi=\frac{22}{7}$]
practice.shortcut: Three circles of $\pi r^2=154$ each → 462. Trap: 308 is only the curved half.

practice.q: The diagonal of a cuboid of dimensions $3\text{ cm}\times4\text{ cm}\times12\text{ cm}$ is:
practice.shortcut: $9+16+144=169=13^2$. This cuboid is a stock triplet (3, 4, 12 → 13).

practice.q: The radius of a cone is 7 cm and its height is 24 cm. Its curved surface area is: [Use $\pi=\frac{22}{7}$]
practice.shortcut: 7-24-25 triplet: $\ell=25$, then $\pi\times7\times25=550$. Trap: 528 uses $h$ instead of $\ell$ ($2\pi rh$).

practice.q: A solid metallic sphere of radius 6 cm is melted and drawn into a cylindrical wire of radius 2 mm. The length of the wire is:
practice.solution:
Sphere: $V=\frac43\pi(6)^3=288\pi$ cu cm.

Wire radius: 2 mm $=0.2$ cm. $V_{\text{wire}}=\pi(0.2)^2L=0.04\pi L$.

$0.04\pi L=288\pi\Rightarrow L=7200$ cm $=72$ m.
practice.shortcut: $288\pi/0.04\pi=7200$ cm. Units trap: 2 mm $=0.2$ cm; answer in metres divides by 100. 720 m forgot that step.

practice.q: A metallic pipe has inner radius 3 cm, outer radius 5 cm and length 14 cm. The volume of metal used is: [Use $\pi=\frac{22}{7}$]
practice.shortcut: Ring area $22\times16=352$, ×14/2... directly: $\frac{22}{7}\times224=704$. Trap: 1100 uses only the outer cylinder.

practice.q: A solid sphere of radius 8 cm is melted and recast into small spheres of radius 1 cm each. The number of small spheres formed is:
practice.shortcut: Cube the radius ratio: $8^3=512$. Trap: 64 (squared the ratio — that is an area ratio).

practice.q: If each edge of a cube increases by 10%, its volume increases by:
practice.shortcut: $1.1^3=1.331$. Trap: 21% is the surface increase; 30% treats volume as linear.

practice.q: A pyramid stands on a square base of side 10 cm and is 12 cm high. Its volume is:
A hemispherical bowl of internal radius 9 cm is full of water. The water is emptied into a cylindrical bottle of radius 3 cm. The height of water in the bottle is: [Use $\pi=\frac{22}{7}$]
practice.shortcut: $486\pi/9\pi=54$. Keep π symbolic — it cancels. Trap: 18 cm uses the bowl volume as $\frac13\pi r^3$.

practice.q: A cube of side 7 cm is painted on all its faces and then cut into 1 cm cubes. How many of the small cubes have exactly two faces painted?
practice.solution: $n=7$: cubes on edges (excluding corners) have exactly two painted faces: $12(n-2)=12\times5=60$.
practice.shortcut: 12 edges × 5 cubes each = 60. Trap: 54 ($6(n-2)^2$ mixing formulas), 75 (5³).
